docs.title: Build a decision. Test it. Release it.
docs.text:
SrotaX evaluates one request document against a Decision Table, Decision Tree, or Flow and returns a result. Start with a shipping policy you can test in Studio and call from Java.

Build your first shipping decision

Build this two-rule shipping policy in the quickstart. Select the screenshot for a full-size view.

docs.title: Choose your task
docs.text: I want to… Start here Define request and response fields Data Contracts Reuse an object structure Models Write ordered business rules Decision Tables Route through conditions Decision Trees Transform lists and call decisions Flows Share and deploy changes Change sets, then Releases Call a released decision from Java Java integration Check expression support Operator reference

docs.title: Understand the lifecycle
docs.text:
Change set → Save draft → Test → Merge into Main → Create release → Activate environment → Execute.

A successful draft test does not deploy a decision. A merge does not activate a release. Runtime calls use the release active in the API key's environment.

This documentation describes the locally verified implementation. See verification and boundaries, including what has not been certified against MongoDB.

docs.title: Build a shipping decision
docs.text:
Create a policy that charges 9 below a subtotal of 100 and offers free shipping at 100 or above. Both rules return the shipping method Standard.

You need an accessible workspace, permission to edit assets, and permission to release/activate and create an API key for the final integration steps. Ask your workspace administrator if these actions are unavailable.

docs.title: 1. Start a change set
docs.text:
Open Change Sets, create a change set named Shipping quickstart, and select it in the workspace header. Main is read-only. In Catalog, choose New Asset → Decision Table, then enter Shipping quickstart.

Choose an editable change set before creating the table. Select any screenshot to open it at full size.

docs.title: 2. Define the contract
docs.text:
Open Data Contract. Under Inputs, expand input and add:

Name Type Required Example subtotal Number Yes 75

Under Outputs, add:

Name Type Required Example fee Number Yes 9 method String Yes Standard

The payload is {"subtotal":75}, not {"input":{"subtotal":75}}. The input. prefix identifies a field inside Studio; it is not an extra envelope your caller supplies.

docs.title: 3. Define two rules
docs.text:
Open Design. Add a condition column for input.subtotal and result columns for output.fee and output.method. Enter the rows in this order:

Row Order subtotal Shipping fee Shipping method 1 Greater than or equal to ($gte) 100 Fixed value 0 Fixed value Standard 2 Less than ($lt) 100 Fixed value 9 Fixed value Standard

The table returns the first matching row. These conditions do not overlap and cover numeric subtotals. This example does not reject negative amounts; add an explicit business rule if that is required.

docs.title: 4. Test boundary values
docs.text:
Open Test Panel → Test Input, enter the JSON below, and choose Run Test:

{"subtotal":75}

Result should contain:

{"fee":9,"method":"Standard"}

Trace identifies row 2 as matched. Also test 0, 99.99, 100, and 150. Subtotals 0, 75, and 99.99 charge 9; 100 and 150 charge 0. Test {"subtotal":"wrong"} and confirm a validation failure. On a change set, testing includes unsaved editor changes.

docs.title: 5. Save and merge
docs.text: Choose Save Draft, then Validate. Open the change set's comparison, check that only your intended rules and contract changed, and merge into Main. Resolve any content conflicts before merging. The asset now has an immutable published version; this is not yet a deployment.

docs.title: 6. Create and activate a release
docs.text:
Open Releases on Main and create a release from its current revision. A release includes the whole workspace Main snapshot, not just this table. For your first walkthrough, use a dedicated workspace or review everything included.

Activate the release in Development. Activation selects the complete release for that environment. It does not change Production.

docs.title: 7. Call it from Java
docs.text: Create a Development API key, copy the asset ID from the asset's API integration information, and run the Java example. Keep the key server-side. The runtime returns an envelope; check success before reading data.

docs.title: Reproducible example
docs.text:
The repository includes examples/shipping/authoring.json and five cases in examples/shipping/cases.json. The automated walkthrough uses real management and runtime HTTP APIs against a disposable database; verification records its scope.

Download the authoring JSON and test cases. The authoring file is for API/fixture use; it is not a claim that Studio has a whole-asset JSON import button.

docs.title: Verification and boundaries
docs.text: This documentation was built against the current local SrotaX code and running services on 2026-10-23/24. The source repositories contain uncommitted work, so a Git commit alone does not identify this exact build. File fingerprints and the operator catalog snapshot are recorded under verification/ and reference/.

docs.title: Shipping journey
docs.text:
scripts/verify-journey.mjs ran against a disposable PostgreSQL database with fixture identity and real Management and Runtime HTTP servers. It verified creation, schema persistence, validation, five preview cases, merge, immutable version retrieval, release creation, activation, five runtime cases, release-linked history, wrong-type failures, invalid-key denial, and the Java HTTP client.

Fixture authentication is test-only. This does not test Google/Microsoft identity providers, production infrastructure, or a customer's permissions configuration. No existing customer release was activated or overwritten.

Browser verification additionally loaded the published table and contract, generated example input, ran the test successfully, confirmed Row 2 matched, and checked Development activation. The quickstart screenshots come from this disposable workspace. Creation, merge, and activation were exercised through HTTP, not by clicking every Studio action.

docs.title: Operator reference
docs.text:
The reference is generated from the actual Management operator catalog. Metadata reports compatibility classifications, source revision, null/missing behavior, signatures, and limitations. These are attributed as engine metadata, not independently certified MongoDB equivalence.

The suite has 34 successful compiler/engine examples and one reproduced known failure.

Selected runnable expression examples are checked against the compiler and engine by scripts/verify-expressions.sh. They do not certify every registered operator or every BSON type. The MongoDB 9.0.4 differential audit records 99 focused cases for the five new operators and 514 broader cases from an earlier catalog snapshot. The broader audit has 108 differences; it has not passed.

docs.title: Build checks
docs.text: Local Markdown links and JSON examples are checked by scripts/check.py. MkDocs strict build validates navigation. The CI workflow repeats these checks; the fixture journey requires a sibling backend build and is documented separately.

docs.title: Known gaps surfaced
docs.text:
• A literal-array $size expression compiled but failed during execution ($size requires one argument). Its operator page and regression fixture record this limitation.
  • Older backend ad-hoc E2E scripts still contain tuple-shaped input fixtures. This new walkthrough uses nested schemas and does not reuse those obsolete payloads.
  • Runtime OpenAPI currently has a generic response schema rather than an exhaustive typed failure contract.
  • Direct Java embedding and broad MongoDB semantic parity are not certified by this documentation.

docs.title: Illustrated guide evidence
docs.text:
The Studio guides include real screenshots from a disposable BrowserFixture, using synthetic shipping and address data. The shipping management/runtime journey was rerun for this update. The additional Tree and Flow examples were prepared with scripts/seed-visual-guides.mjs; preview calls returned fee 9 / Standard and total 84 respectively for subtotal 75. These checks cover those inputs, not every branch or UI interaction.

Screenshots demonstrate the Catalog, change-set selection, contract reference, Models editor, OpenAPI selection dialog, Tree branches and condition drawer, and a simple Flow. They are not a claim that every illustrated task has a complete automated browser test.

docs.title: Call SrotaX from Java
docs.text: Use Java's HTTP client to execute a decision through the Runtime API. This approach does not embed the engine or require a SrotaX SDK.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Merge the decision, create a release, activate it in the API key's environment, and obtain that environment's key. Use the decision's stable ID, not its display name. Set these environment variables through your deployment's secret configuration:

  • SROTAX_RUNTIME_URL: runtime origin, for example https://runtime.example.com.
  • SROTAX_DECISION_ID: decision UUID.
  • SROTAX_API_KEY: runtime key. Do not put it in frontend code or source control.

The repository's examples/java/ShippingClient.java works on Java 17+ and was executed with Java 21 against the disposable runtime.

java examples/java/ShippingClient.java

The sample sends {"subtotal":75} and prints the JSON response. It checks HTTP status; your application must also parse the response using its JSON library and check success == true before using data. For the shipping example, data is {"fee":9,"method":"Standard"}.

Download ShippingClient.java

import java.net.URI;
import java.net.http.*;
import java.time.Duration;

/** Java 17+; API key stays in the environment. The response is a JSON envelope. */
public class ShippingClient {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        String base = required("SROTAX_RUNTIME_URL").replaceAll("/$", "");
        String decision = required("SROTAX_DECISION_ID");
        var client = HttpClient.newBuilder().connectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5)).build();
        var request = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create(base + "/api/runtime/decisions/" + decision + "/execute"))
            .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(30))
            .header("Authorization", "Bearer " + required("SROTAX_API_KEY"))
            .header("Content-Type", "application/json")
            .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString("{\"subtotal\":75}"))
            .build();
        var response = client.send(request, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString());
        if (response.statusCode() != 200) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("SrotaX HTTP status " + response.statusCode());
        }
        // The calling application must also parse and check `success` before using `data`.
        System.out.println(response.body());
    }
    private static String required(String name) {
        String value = System.getenv(name);
        if (value == null || value.isBlank()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Missing " + name);
        return value;
    }
}

docs.title: Handle failures
docs.text:
A transport failure or timeout is not a business result. An HTTP 200 response may still describe a failed execution. Keep these paths distinct. See Runtime API.

The sample uses a 5-second connection timeout and 30-second request timeout as example client settings; these do not configure server limits. Choose them based on your deployment. Do not blindly retry a Flow containing external side effects: a timeout does not prove it never ran.

docs.title: Embedding is a separate integration
docs.text: This guide verifies remote execution only. Direct JVM engine embedding does not automatically provide SrotaX release loading, workspace permissions, API-key scope, reference data, or dependency resolution. A supported embedding contract needs separate verification before it belongs in this guide.

docs.title: Runtime API
docs.text:
Send one JSON document to:

POST /api/runtime/decisions/{decisionId}/execute
Authorization: Bearer <runtime-api-key>
Content-Type: application/json

The key determines organisation, workspace, and environment. Do not send those as body fields to select another scope. The request body is the decision's input document.

docs.title: Successful execution
docs.text: The response includes success, data, and execution metadata such as runId. Check success before using data; preserve runId for troubleshooting. Do not assume every HTTP 200 is a successful decision evaluation.

docs.title: Verified failure cases
docs.text:
Case Observed behavior Invalid API key HTTP 401 No active release containing the asset HTTP 404 Wrong type for required input Failed execution; no successful result

These cases are verified by the documentation walkthrough. Other limits and error details are deployment-specific; do not treat this table as an exhaustive HTTP error schema.

The runtime OpenAPI document currently describes a generic response object. Applications should not assume an undocumented exhaustive generated error model. The source snapshot is reference/runtime-openapi.json in the documentation repository.

Download the runtime OpenAPI snapshot.

docs.title: Statistics and bitwise expressions
docs.text:
Use these expression operators inside a Set Fields calculation. They calculate a value from one request document; they are not pipeline stages and do not require splitting a list into documents.

The engine registers all five operators, the compiler accepts their expression forms, and the API catalog exposes them in the Visual expression editor. The JSON examples below are also supported. These additions do not add new Aggregate List palette choices.

docs.title: Calculate statistics from a list
docs.text:
For this request:

{"amounts": [10, 20, 30, 40]}

Use $amounts in the generated document expression. In Studio's field picker this is input.amounts. Store the calculation in a declared local.* or output.* field. Reading the list does not modify the immutable input.

Operator Purpose Result for this input $median Middle value using the discrete percentile rule 20 $percentile Values at selected probabilities [10, 20, 40] for [0, 0.5, 1] $stdDevPop Spread when this list is the entire population Approximately 11.1803398875 $stdDevSamp Estimated spread when this list is a sample Approximately 12.9099444874

docs.title: Median
docs.text:
{"$median": {"input": "$amounts", "method": "approximate"}}

For an even number of values, this implementation matches the tested MongoDB 9.0.4 expression behavior: it selects the lower middle value, not the average of the two middle values. Thus [10,20,30,40] returns 20, not 25.

docs.title: Percentiles
docs.text:
{"$percentile": {"input": "$amounts", "p": [0, 0.5, 1], "method": "approximate"}}

The result is always an array, ordered like p. Each probability must be between 0 and 1, inclusive. p cannot be empty. 0 selects the minimum; 1 selects the maximum. Other probabilities select the sorted value at index ceil(p × count) - 1, clamped to the first value.

In Visual mode choose a fixed array for p and the fixed text approximate for method. In SrotaX's JSON editor, p must also be a literal array. The engine can evaluate some constant expressions for p, but the authoring compiler deliberately accepts the literal form only. A document-field reference is not supported for p.

The method name is required for MongoDB syntax compatibility. Fluxion sorts the values and uses discrete selection for the document expression; it does not implement MongoDB's cross-document approximate accumulator algorithm.

docs.title: Population and sample deviation
docs.text:
{"$stdDevPop": "$amounts"}

{"$stdDevSamp": "$amounts"}

Choose population deviation when the list contains the full population you want to describe. Choose sample deviation when estimating a larger population from a sample. Sample deviation divides by n - 1; population deviation divides by n.

A single operand resolving to a list traverses its numeric elements. With multiple operands, each operand is considered separately and array-valued operands are ignored. For example:

{"$stdDevSamp": [10, 20, 30]}

This returns 10. To express a literal list as one operand explicitly, use {"$literal": [10,20,30]} as shown in the individual operator examples.

docs.title: Empty and mixed inputs
docs.text:
Input case Median / percentile Population deviation Sample deviation Empty, missing, null, or no numeric values null / one null per requested percentile null null One numeric value That value / repeated for each percentile 0 null Mixed strings, booleans, objects, nested lists Ignore nonnumeric elements Ignore nonnumeric elements Ignore nonnumeric elements Numeric scalar Treat as one value 0 null

For BSON inputs containing special numeric values, median/percentile ignore NaN and retain infinities. Standard deviation can produce NaN for nonfinite values. Ordinary JSON cannot represent NaN or infinity; avoid these values in HTTP request examples.

docs.title: Bitwise NOT
docs.text:
$bitNot flips every bit in a signed integer. It is not Boolean NOT; use $not for a true/false condition.

{"$bitNot": {"$toInt": 5}}

Result:

-6

In two's complement, ~x = -x - 1. The operator preserves a 32-bit or 64-bit integer's width. Missing/null returns null. Double, Decimal128, string, Boolean, and array operands are rejected. Use $toInt or $toLong deliberately when the source is not already an integer; conversion can truncate a fractional value or fail on overflow. Visual number literals may be represented as decimals, so nest a conversion before Bitwise NOT.

docs.title: MongoDB compatibility boundary
docs.text:
The focused differential test used a real MongoDB 9.0.4 process: 99 cases, 80 matching values, and 19 inputs rejected by both engines. It checked empty/missing/null values, mixed arrays, odd/even lengths, scalar inputs, Decimal128 values, nonfinite values, percentile bounds, invalid options, and integer widths.

This is evidence for the tested single-document expression forms, not complete MongoDB compatibility:

  • No new $group accumulators or $setWindowFields variants are provided by this change.
  • Standard deviation uses double arithmetic and comparisons allow a relative tolerance of 1e-12; bit-for-bit equality for all numeric inputs is not promised.
  • MongoDB error codes and messages are not reproduced.
  • The compiler requires literal percentile options; it does not accept every constant-expression spelling supported by MongoDB.
  • Locale/collation, storage/query operators, and distributed accumulation are outside this feature.

See the broader audit for existing operator differences. The checked-in evidence is verification/statistics-mongo-9.0.4.json; rerun the opt-in StatisticsMongoParityTest in fluxion-core-engine against MongoDB 9.0.4 to reproduce it.

docs.title: Condition recipes
docs.text: These are SrotaX condition recipes from the API catalog. Some combine multiple engine operators; recipe names must not be presented as MongoDB operators.

docs.title: Combine conditions with nested groups
docs.text:
Use AND when every condition must pass and OR when any condition may pass. A nested group lets you combine those choices in one rule.

This Decision Tree condition requires a subtotal greater than 100 and a country of either CA or US:

subtotal > 100 AND (country = CA OR country = US)

The outer AND combines the subtotal comparison with the entire nested OR group.

  1. Open a Decision Tree condition and select AND for its outer group.
  2. Select input.subtotal, Greater than, and 100.
  3. Select Add group and choose OR within the nested group.
  4. Add input.country Equals CA and input.country Equals US inside that group.
  5. Save the draft and test both matching and nonmatching inputs.
Subtotal Country Condition result 150 CA True 150 US True 150 GB False 100 CA False: the comparison is strictly greater than 100

Keep both country checks inside the nested group. Putting all three comparisons in an outer OR group would allow CA or US orders regardless of their subtotal.

docs.title: Expressions
docs.text: Visual expressions choose a supported function and supply its arguments. Advanced JSON expressions use the engine's expression syntax. The modes contain separate expressions: select the one you intend to use. They are not automatically synchronized.

docs.title: Read an expression
docs.text:
This example uses Add ($add) with two numeric Fixed value arguments: 75 and 9. The result is 84, assigned to output.total by the Set Fields step.

Edit mode with the function catalog expanded. Browse categories on the left, scroll or search the function list, and configure arguments on the right. Select Choose function to reopen the catalog after choosing a function.

To configure this example in a Flow, open Set Fields, select output.total, choose Use expression, and open Edit expression. In Visual mode, select Add, then provide the two number arguments. Select Done to update the step and Save Draft to save the asset. Run a test and check that output.total is 84.

docs.title: Field scope and testing
docs.text:
input.*, local.*, output.*, and the current list item have different scopes. Select fields from the picker where possible. A reference that exists in another step or another asset is not automatically available at the current location.

The operator inventory separates registered engine operators from functions offered to the Visual editor. Scoped operators such as $map, $filter, and $reduce require scope-aware configuration and are not generic Visual function entries.

Condition pickers also contain business-facing recipes built from one or more operators. A recipe name does not necessarily identify a MongoDB operator. Use condition reference to inspect their metadata.

For each expression, test its normal value, null/missing inputs, wrong types, and boundary values relevant to your contract. Structural validation cannot establish that the formula is your intended business rule.

docs.title: MongoDB compatibility: tested scope
docs.text:
Historical baseline: the results below predate the current all-operator behavior and parity suite. Use each operator page for current observed behavior and differences.

SrotaX is a single-document decision and transformation engine. MongoDB operator names are not a guarantee of identical behavior. Catalog registration, authoring-compiler support, and parity tests are separate checks.

docs.title: New statistics and bitwise operators
docs.text: The five new expressions passed 99 focused comparisons against MongoDB 9.0.4: 80 matching results and 19 inputs rejected by both engines. Results allow a relative floating-point tolerance of 1e-12; error-code and message parity remain unverified.

docs.title: Broader existing-operator audit
docs.text:
A separate audit of an earlier 119-operator Visual catalog snapshot ran 514 cases against MongoDB 9.0.4. It produced 284 exact BSON matches, 122 cases rejected by both engines, and 108 differences. This snapshot is not the complete current catalog. The count is a number of test cases, not a number of unsupported operators.

Differences can be result values, BSON result types, document field order, null/missing behavior, or accepting an input MongoDB rejects. Some differences are representation-only; they are not all wrong business values. They are recorded as open compatibility gaps; the five new operators do not fix these existing differences. The exact-case report is checked in at verification/mongodb-9.0.4-audit.json.

Examples from the report:

Case MongoDB 9.0.4 Fluxion $add of integer 2 and 3 Integer 5 Double 5.0; same numeric value, different BSON type $filter with limit: 1 over [1,2,3] and a true condition [1] [1,2,3]; limit not respected $anyElementTrue with null operand Error false $toBool with an empty argument list Error true $regexFind for ab in abc Fields ordered match, idx, captures Same values with a different field order Existing operator Differing test cases $abs 1 $acos 2 $acosh 2 $add 5 $allElementsTrue 3 $anyElementTrue 3 $arrayElemAt 1 $arrayToObject 1 $asin 2 $asinh 2 $atan 2 $atan2 2 $atanh 2 $cond 1 $convert 2 $cos 2 $cosh 2 $degreesToRadians 2 $exp 2 $filter 2 $first 1 $getField 1 $ifNull 1 $indexOfBytes 2 $last 1 $let 1 $ln 2 $log 2 $log10 2 $map 1 $min 2 $mod 1 $multiply 2 $objectToArray 2 $pow 1 $radiansToDegrees 2 $range 1 $reduce 1 $regexFind 3 $regexFindAll 3 $reverseArray 1 $round 2 $setDifference 2 $setUnion 2 $sin 2 $sinh 2 $slice 2 $split 2 $strcasecmp 2 $substr 2 $substrBytes 2 $substrCP 2 $subtract 1 $sum 4 $tan 2 $tanh 2 $toBool 1 $tsIncrement 1 $tsSecond 1

docs.title: Product scope labels
docs.text:
Use these labels when interpreting the MongoDB inventory:

Label Meaning Capabilities Out of scope by design Deliberately excluded from the processing engine; not missing implementation work Native UUID/ObjectId types, indexed text/vector search, search-index management, database/cluster administration, and writes to database collections Deferred Outside the current implementation; intended for later stream orchestration Source/sink connectors, continuous consumption, checkpoints, retries, backpressure, and delivery guarantees Not supported yet An unimplemented processing capability, without a delivery commitment Applicable document/array operators and the conversion extensions listed below Compatibility difference An implemented operator differs from MongoDB in tested behavior The observed cases in the differential audit

$search, $searchMeta, $vectorSearch, and $listSearchIndexes are Out of scope by design, as are database administration stages and collection-writing $merge/$out. Search and database access can be performed by an external integration that supplies input to the engine.

Do not classify calculations over vectors already supplied in a document as indexed vector search. Do not classify in-memory document/array processing as stream orchestration. Stage syntax alone does not determine product scope.

docs.title: Remaining expression-name inventory
docs.text:
Relative to the MongoDB 9.0.4 inventory checked on this feature branch, 151 of 167 expression names are shared after the thirteen array/statistics/JSON conversion additions. Fluxion registers 159 expression names in total, including eight extensions or names used in another MongoDB context. These 16 names are absent from the compared expression registry; all 16 are Out of scope by design, not a backlog of missing features:

$createObjectId, $encStrContains, $encStrEndsWith, $encStrNormalizedEq, $encStrStartsWith, $hash, $hexHash, $meta, $rand, $sampleRate, $sigmoid, $similarityCosine, $similarityDotProduct, $similarityEuclidean, $toHashedIndexKey, $toUUID.

This list is an inventory, not a proposed roadmap. Storage/encryption/search metadata and nondeterministic expressions may not fit SrotaX's deterministic single-document purpose. Adding a name would still require behavior and compiler tests. Pipeline-stage and cross-document accumulator gaps are not addressed by these expressions.

docs.title: Interpreting these results
docs.text:
Test the complete expression with realistic boundary inputs before relying on MongoDB-equivalent behavior. A passing example does not cover all BSON types, arities, Unicode strings, numeric boundaries, or invalid inputs. “Both rejected” establishes rejection only, not equivalent errors. The broad audit compares BSON exactly; the focused statistics suite uses a documented numeric tolerance, so their match counts use different criteria.

The broader parity test is opt-in (Mongo9CompatibilityAuditTest with FLUXION_AUDIT_MONGO_URI). It fails when it sees a difference; report-only mode is for investigating gaps, not claiming parity. Normal engine unit tests do not substitute for this differential check.

docs.title: Unsupported conversion extensions
docs.text:
The presence of $convert does not imply support for all MongoDB conversion options. These capabilities are currently unavailable in SrotaX:

  • UUID string ↔ binary UUID and $toUUID: Out of scope by design (native identifier types).
  • Base64, Base64URL, hex, UTF-8, or UUID string ↔ binary conversions.
  • Numeric value ↔ binary bytes, including configurable byte order.
  • binData conversion targets and binary subtype selection.
  • $convert options format, byteOrder, and base, including newer conversion-format variants.

Perform these conversions in the calling application or integration layer if needed. UUID identifiers can remain ordinary strings when no binary representation is required. Existing supported conversions remain available. $bitNot is supported and is not included in this list.

Copilot's authoring instructions include these exclusions. For a request that requires an unsupported conversion, the instructed response is status=unsupported with no authoring proposal and a specific explanation. This prompt guidance does not guarantee every model response will comply; backend validation remains necessary.

docs.title: Ranked array selection
docs.text: $topN is now supported as a single-document array expression. It delegates to the existing $sortArray and $firstN implementations. See the executed example. Accumulator and window forms remain unsupported; collation and exact MongoDB error parity are not certified.

docs.title: Native identifier types: Out of scope by design
docs.text:
Native UUID (binary subtype 4) and BSON ObjectId data types are Out of scope by design for SrotaX authoring. They are not missing/planned product features. Represent identifiers as ordinary strings in contracts, models, inputs, local fields, and outputs; callers can validate/normalize strings and perform native-type conversion at integration boundaries.

This scope decision includes $toUUID, $createObjectId, $toObjectId, and $convert targeting native UUID/ObjectId values (including BSON type code 7 and UUID binary subtype 4). Copilot should direct requests for these native types to an external integration rather than generate them.

Ordinary Object data remains supported: nested JSON fields, models, and responses are not ObjectId values. $toObject is a separate object-conversion capability, not an identifier conversion.

This is a product-scope classification, not a claim that all corresponding engine code is absent. Existing low-level ObjectId conversion support is still present; this documentation change does not remove or disable it.

docs.title: JSON string containers
docs.text: $toArray, $toObject, and $convert targeting array/object share strict JSON parsing. Null/missing input returns null; invalid input raises a conversion error or uses $convert.onError. Binary-vector conversion remains unsupported. Verified with 76 focused MongoDB 9.0.4 comparison cases; error-code parity is not claimed.

docs.title: Remaining expression operators: Out of scope by design
docs.text:
All 16 absent expression names in the MongoDB 9.0.4 comparison are Out of scope by design. They are deliberately excluded from the current product scope, not planned implementation work.

Category Operators Hashing $hash, $hexHash, $toHashedIndexKey Scoring $sigmoid Vector calculations $similarityCosine, $similarityDotProduct, $similarityEuclidean Randomness $rand, $sampleRate Encrypted-field matching $encStrContains, $encStrEndsWith, $encStrNormalizedEq, $encStrStartsWith Metadata $meta Native identifiers $createObjectId, $toUUID

Perform these operations in the caller or an external integration when needed. Vector calculations are excluded by product choice, even when vectors are already present in the input; this is separate from indexed vector search.

The scope decision applies to these expression operators. The custom Fluxion $sampleRate stage has also been removed; do not generate it in any context. Expression-name coverage remains 151 of 167 MongoDB names. This classification does not establish full compatibility: behavioral differences in supported operators still require verification and fixes. Stage, accumulator and window-function gaps retain their separate classifications.

The former custom $agentCall stage has been removed from Fluxion Core. Agent invocation belongs in an external integration/orchestration layer. This does not remove SrotaX Copilot for authoring decisions.

docs.title: How to read the operator reference
docs.text:
Each operator page has two independent parts:

  1. SrotaX behavior: definition, syntax, plain-language parameters, behavior, runnable examples and downloadable regression cases. Full input matrices are collapsed by default.
  2. MongoDB differences: a separately marked final section with live comparison results and exact evidence.

The behavior tables are the documented contract for their tested inputs. They do not promise behavior for every input combination. Metadata types are authoring hints; observed runtime behavior can be broader or stricter. A compiler or Data Contract may reject an input before it reaches the engine.

docs.title: Current coverage
docs.text:
The live comparison used MongoDB 9.0.4 and the Core source snapshot identified in the evidence. It ran 6,495 cases for 159 registered expression operators:

Outcome Cases Exact result, including BSON types 2,100 Both implementations rejected the expression 3,360 Different value, type, missing/null behavior, or acceptance 697 Same typed values; different object field order 7 Extension or different MongoDB context; not compared 331

99 operators have at least one observed difference. This suite does not establish full MongoDB compatibility. For example, an int32 result and an equal-valued double are reported as different. Both-rejected cases do not establish matching error codes or messages.

The eight names not compared as MongoDB expressions are $coalesce, $endsWith, $expr, $minDistance, $nin, $nor, $setIsSuperset, and $startsWith.

docs.title: Interpreting the input tables
docs.text:
For each argument, the test replaces only that argument in the page's example. All others stay the same. Null means an explicitly null value; missing means an absent field. Typed dates and Decimal128 use Extended JSON in the downloadable input document. Ordinary JSON strings remain strings.

Tables include numeric, string, boolean, object and array inputs, empty values, mixed arrays and null/missing cases. Advertised optional named arguments are also probed individually, including options absent from the baseline. These are individual substitutions, not the cross-product of every argument, timezone, locale or option.

Scope: expression evaluation inside a document. Pipeline stages, grouping accumulators and window functions need their own suites. Live results do not certify Studio authoring of every expression or complete released Flow execution.

The JVM timezone is fixed to America/Toronto and locale to en-IN. Some older calendar operators use these defaults. Object field order is recorded in live comparisons but ignored by the engine regression baseline because some returned maps have unstable ordering. Array order and BSON numeric types remain significant.

docs.title: Resource boundaries
docs.text: An extreme $range endpoint exhausted the test JVM heap. This is documented on that operator's page. The bounded matrix excludes allocation stress cases; resource limits need separate process-isolated tests.

docs.title: Maintaining the reference
docs.text:
Core's AllOperatorParityTest verifies engine results against the checked-in behavior baseline. A deliberate behavior change requires reviewing affected examples, refreshing live comparison evidence and regenerating these pages. The documentation's local-link, JSON and strict-build checks validate publication structure, not engine semantics.

Operator pages are generated by scripts/generate-operator-behavior.py using verification/all-operator-behavior.json. The evidence records source and case hashes. The general reference generator invokes the behavior generator so metadata-only generation cannot overwrite verified behavior.

To omit all MongoDB sections while keeping SrotaX behavior:

python scripts/generate-operator-behavior.py \
  --report verification/all-operator-behavior.json --without-mongo

To remove only one page's comparison section, delete the block between BEGIN MONGO PARITY and END MONGO PARITY. Regeneration restores it unless the omission option is used.

docs.title: Stage reference
docs.text:
The stage reference follows the same structure. Its 86 cases cover all 21 registered Core stages and run through PipelineExecutor with a fresh context. These are Core behavior checks, not live MongoDB stage parity tests.

Regenerate both reference sections and the grouped navigation:

python scripts/generate-reference.py

Use --without-mongo to omit the comparison blocks from both operators and stages. Keep reference/stage-catalog.json prose and examples/stages.json examples aligned with the implementation. Stage verification runs with JDK 21 and the Core build:

mvn -f ../fluxion-core-engine/pom.xml test-compile dependency:build-classpath -Dmdep.outputFile=target/docs-classpath.txt
sh scripts/verify-stages.sh

The verifier compares actual results against verification/stage-behavior.json. Its --record option refreshes evidence only after intentional changes have been reviewed. Generated pages must not be edited by hand.

docs.title: Supported schema format
docs.text:
Models and contract sections use nested OpenAPI-style Schema Objects. The supported subset is intentionally narrower than unrestricted OpenAPI or JSON Schema.

{
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "subtotal": {"type": "number", "example": 75},
    "customer": {
      "type": "object",
      "properties": {"name": {"type": "string"}},
      "required": ["name"]
    },
    "items": {"type": "array", "items": {"type": "string"}}
  },
  "required": ["subtotal"]
}
Feature Supported representation Object type: object, properties, optional required array Scalar string, number, boolean Date/time type: string, format: date-time List type: array, items schema; {} permits unspecified item type Metadata title, description, example where accepted Model reference $ref: #/components/schemas/{modelId}

Stored refs use model UUIDs, not names. OpenAPI import/export converts readable external component names at the boundary. $ref objects cannot add sibling custom fields. Examples must match scalar types.

Unsupported keywords are rejected, including unrestricted oneOf, allOf, anyOf, enum, validation constraints such as minimum, and arbitrary additionalProperties. Use a decision or validation step for business constraints supported by the editor. integer is not a separate accepted scalar type here; use number.

Property names must match [A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*. The current parser enforces a 64-field limit and nesting checks; model resolution also checks expanded references and cycles. Do not use recursive schemas.

This page is derived from srotax-core/SchemaContracts.java and model resolution, not a claim of full OpenAPI conformance.

docs.title: Aggregation stages
docs.text:
Stages transform a list of documents. Expression operators calculate a value inside a document. The same name can have different syntax in these contexts.

These pages describe the 21 registered Core stages. They are not a list of Studio palette steps. For the authoring UI, use the Flow step reference. SrotaX normally processes one request document; use array expressions such as $map and $sortArray to transform its lists.

Each page includes a runnable pipeline, actual Core output, and implementation limits. The stage examples are separate from the 6,495-case expression parity suite.

Stage Purpose $match Retains documents that satisfy a condition object. $addFields Adds or replaces fields while retaining other fields. $set Adds or replaces fields while retaining other fields. $project Builds each output document from explicitly selected or computed fields. $unset Removes named fields from each document. $limit Keeps the first N documents. $skip Drops the first N documents. $sort Orders documents by one or more fields. $unwind Produces one document for each element of an array field. $replaceRoot Replaces the entire document with an object expression. $replaceWith Replaces the entire document with an object expression. $group Combines documents sharing a grouping key and computes accumulator outputs. $sortByCount Counts documents per grouping value and sorts groups by descending count. $bucket Groups numeric values into explicit lower-inclusive, upper-exclusive ranges. $bucketAuto Divides the numeric value range into equal-width buckets. $facet Runs named child pipelines over the same input list and collects their results. $lookup Adds matching records from a host-provided in-memory dataset. $densify Inserts documents for missing numeric or date positions. $fill Replaces null or missing values using a value expression or interpolation. $setWindowFields Adds values computed over an ordered partition of documents. $subPipeline Executes inline child pipelines or resolves child references through the caller’s execution context.

docs.title: Flow step reference
docs.text:
Configure steps using available contract fields and compatible local destinations. This is a task reference for Studio operations; it is not a promise that every MongoDB aggregation stage is exposed.

Step Purpose Important configuration Request Start with the incoming document Input contract Validate Data Check required values and types Fields to validate and behavior Set Fields Assign fixed values, copies, or expressions Destination and source/expression; never write input.* Choose Fields Select the fields retained in a working/result object Source and retained fields; input remains immutable Transform Each Item Map list items Source list, item expression/mapping, destination Filter List Keep matching items Source list, item conditions, destination Flatten List Flatten nested lists Source and destination Sort List Order list items Sort fields/directions; in-place only for local lists Trim List Keep a range or count Source, range/count, destination Aggregate List Calculate a list summary List, operation, value field, destination Check Exists Test whether matching items exist List, predicate, boolean destination Lookup Read reference-data values Dataset/version, key mapping, result destination If / Else Route by conditions Conditions and complete outgoing branches Decision Table / Decision Tree Call a decision asset Dependency, input mappings, result destination Call Flow Call a reusable Flow Dependency, input mappings, result destination Response Return the chosen response Response mapping/shape compatible with Outputs

Do not infer support for collection-level stages such as $merge or $out from MongoDB documentation. Use the editor's actual palette and validate the completed Flow. Operator registration alone does not establish that a stage is available in Studio.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Converts input to a named target type with optional fallbacks.

Expression operator · Types and conversion · Studio Visual: available. Studio validates the complete expression separately.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
{
  "$convert": {
    "input": <input>,
    "to": <to>,
    "onError": <onError>,
    "onNull": <onNull>
  }
}

Replace angle-bracket placeholders with expressions or values.

Optional parameters may be omitted.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Required Description input Yes Expression supplying the value to process. A field reference such as "$price" reads from the current document. to Yes Target type name or numeric type code. See Supported values below; for example, "int" or 16. onError No Fallback expression for a supported conversion/parsing failure. If omitted, that failure raises an error. onNull No Fallback expression for null or missing input. If omitted, the null-input result is null.

Supported to target names: array, object, bool, double, string, date, int, long, decimal. Array/object conversion parses a JSON string with the matching root. onError supplies a conversion-failure fallback; onNull supplies a null/missing fallback. Native ObjectId and UUID authoring remain outside the supported SrotaX scope.

docs.title: Supported values
docs.text:
to accepts a numeric BSON type code or a string type name. Names are case-sensitive: use "int" or "string", not "INT" or "STRING".

String target Numeric code Result "double" 1 Floating-point number "string" 2 String "object" 3 Object parsed from a JSON object string, existing object inputs are rejected "array" 4 Array parsed from a JSON array string, existing array inputs are rejected "bool" 8 Boolean "date" 9 Date "int" 16 Signed 32-bit integer "long" 18 Signed 64-bit integer "decimal" 19 Decimal number

Core additionally implements "objectId" / 7, but native ObjectId authoring is outside SrotaX product scope. UUID is not a supported target.

For example, these first two expressions both convert "42" to an integer; the third converts 42 to a string: 

{
  "$convert": {
    "input": "42",
    "to": "int"
  }
}


{
  "$convert": {
    "input": "42",
    "to": 16
  }
}

{
  "$convert": {
    "input": 42,
    "to": "string"
  }
}

With a non-null input, an unsupported string target throws unless onError is supplied. Unsupported numeric codes throw before onError is evaluated. A null input returns onNull (or null) before checking the target; a null target with non-null input returns null.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Parses a date string and returns a date value.

Expression operator · Dates · Studio Visual: available. Studio validates the complete expression separately.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
{
  "$dateFromString": {
    "dateString": <dateString>,
    "format": <format>,
    "timezone": <timezone>,
    "onError": <onError>,
    "onNull": <onNull>
  }
}

Replace angle-bracket placeholders with expressions or values.

Optional parameters may be omitted.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Required Description dateString Yes Expression supplying a date string to parse. format No Date format string. See Supported values below for the tokens implemented by this operator. timezone No Timezone name or offset used for the calendar operation, for example "America/Toronto" or "+05:30". Defaults to UTC when omitted. onError No Fallback expression for a supported conversion/parsing failure. If omitted, that failure raises an error. onNull No Fallback expression for null or missing input. If omitted, the null-input result is null.

docs.title: Supported values
docs.text: Supported format tokens: %Y, %m, %d, %H, %M, %S, %L, %j, %G, %V, %u, %z, %%. Unsupported tokens raise an error. For example, %Y-%m-%d represents year-month-day.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Subtracts a calendar amount and returns a date value.

Expression operator · Dates · Studio Visual: available. Studio validates the complete expression separately.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
{
  "$dateSubtract": {
    "startDate": <startDate>,
    "unit": <unit>,
    "amount": <amount>,
    "timezone": <timezone>
  }
}

Replace angle-bracket placeholders with expressions or values.

Optional parameters may be omitted.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Required Description startDate Yes Expression supplying the starting date. unit Yes Time unit name, such as "day" or "hour". See Supported values below. amount Yes Number of time units to add or subtract. timezone No Timezone name or offset used for the calendar operation, for example "America/Toronto" or "+05:30". Defaults to UTC when omitted.

docs.title: Supported values
docs.text: unit: "year", "quarter", "month", "week", "day", "hour", "minute", "second", "millisecond". Names are case-sensitive. An omitted timezone defaults to UTC for these named date operators. Where supported, startOfWeek defaults to Sunday and accepts full weekday names or three-letter abbreviations, case-insensitively.

docs.title: Definition

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Groups numeric values into explicit lower-inclusive, upper-exclusive ranges.

Core aggregation stage · Group and summarize. Use this syntax in a Core pipeline; Studio availability depends on the Flow compiler.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
Basic form, with concrete values: 

{
  "$bucket": {
    "groupBy": "$price",
    "boundaries": [
      0,
      10,
      20
    ],
    "default": "other",
    "output": {
      "count": {
        "$sum": 1
      }
    }
  }
}

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Required Description groupBy Yes Expression resolving to the numeric value to classify. boundaries Yes At least two numeric boundaries in ascending order. Adjacent values define ranges. default No Label for values outside the ranges or for nonnumeric/null/missing values. output No Accumulator output fields. Omitted output produces only _id; explicitly add count with $sum: 1.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
• Only populated buckets appear, in boundary order followed by the default bucket.
  • Without a default, unmatched values are skipped.
  • Boundary comparison uses doubles. Use a fresh context for independent requests.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Divides the numeric value range into equal-width buckets.

Core aggregation stage · Group and summarize. Use this syntax in a Core pipeline; Studio availability depends on the Flow compiler.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
Basic form, with concrete values: 

{
  "$bucketAuto": {
    "groupBy": "$price",
    "buckets": 2,
    "output": {
      "count": {
        "$sum": 1
      }
    }
  }
}

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Required Description groupBy Yes Numeric expression used to compute the value range. Nonnumeric values are ignored. buckets Yes Positive integer number of buckets. output No Supported accumulators: $sum, $avg, $min, $max, $push, $addToSet, $first, $last. No default count is added.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
• This implementation uses equal-width ranges, not equal document populations.
  • Each _id is the numeric lower bound. Empty buckets can appear. The final upper bound is maximum + 1.
  • With no numeric values the output is empty. Granularity is not implemented.

docs.text: Parameter Required Description from Yes Array/object of foreign records, or a dataset name provided in execution globals under foreignCollections. localField Yes Local join field path. foreignField Yes Foreign join field path. as No Output field containing matched foreign records. docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Orders documents by one or more fields.

Core aggregation stage · Filter and order. Use this syntax in a Core pipeline; Studio availability depends on the Flow compiler.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
Basic form, with concrete values: 

{
  "$sort": {
    "score": -1,
    "name": 1
  }
}

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Required Description field: direction Yes Sort field path and direction: 1 ascending or -1 descending. Fields are compared in specification order.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
• Sorts the document list, not an array inside one document. Use the $sortArray expression for an array.
  • Equal keys keep their incoming order. Missing/null values sort before non-null values in ascending order.
  • Unsupported comparison values fall back to their string representations. There is no database collation setting.

docs.title: Empty input and invalid specification
docs.text:
These cases use the basic form above unless the specification is explicitly replaced.

Case Observed result empty input [] invalid specification (null) Error: IllegalArgumentException — $sort expects an object with sort keys

Input documents: 

[
  {
    "name": "B",
    "score": 2
  },
  {
    "name": "A",
    "score": 3
  }
]

Pipeline: 

[
  {
    "$sort": {
      "score": -1,
      "name": 1
    }
  }
]

Result: 

[
  {
    "name": "A",
    "score": 3
  },
  {
    "name": "B",
    "score": 2
  }
]

docs.title: Invalid direction
docs.text:
Input documents: 

[
  {
    "score": 1
  },
  {
    "score": 2
  }
]

Pipeline: 

[
  {
    "$sort": {
      "score": 0
    }
  }
]

Observed error: $sort direction must be 1 or -1: 0

Input documents: 

[
  {
    "score": 2
  },
  {
    "score": null
  },
  {}
]

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Counts documents per grouping value and sorts groups by descending count.

Core aggregation stage · Group and summarize. Use this syntax in a Core pipeline; Studio availability depends on the Flow compiler.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Required Description expression Yes Expression used as the grouping key.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
• Internally executes $group with a count followed by $sort on count descending.
  • Output fields are _id and count. Equal-count ordering is not a business ordering guarantee.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Executes inline child pipelines or resolves child references through the caller’s execution context.

Core aggregation stage · Core extensions. Use this syntax in a Core pipeline; Studio availability depends on the Flow compiler.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
Basic form, with concrete values: 

{
  "$subPipeline": [
    {
      "pipeline": [
        {
          "$set": {
            "approved": true
          }
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Required Description steps Yes Array of child entries, executed sequentially. pipeline or ref One per child Inline stage array or reference resolved by the host. version can accompany ref. input No Expression selecting child input documents. output No Destination for a child result; mapped children must return exactly one document. when No Boolean expression controlling whether a child runs. globals No Child global-variable overrides. onError No "bubble", "skip", or inherited behavior. parallel / merge No Parallel child array; merge modes "concat", "zip", or "facet".

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
• A reference requires a resolver in the execution context; there is no global pipeline registry.
  • Mapped output preserves the parent and inserts the child result.
  • This is the Core mechanism behind host-managed composition. Configure SrotaX asset dependencies through Call Flow, not raw registry names.

docs.title: Definition

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Produces one document for each element of an array field.

Core aggregation stage · Reshape documents. Use this syntax in a Core pipeline; Studio availability depends on the Flow compiler.

docs.title: Syntax

docs.text:

  • A non-null scalar emits the original document once.
  • Nested field handling uses shallow copies; prefer array expressions for document-local list transformations.
